main.title: The Marriage of Maria Braun
main.subtitle: An absent marriage runs through the years of reconstruction
main.summary: Rainer Werner Fassbinder's The Marriage of Maria Braun follows a woman building a place for herself in post-war West Germany while remaining attached to an absent husband. Hanna Schygulla plays Maria, who marries Hermann near the end of the war. The film premiered publicly at the Berlin International Film Festival on 20 February 1979, after being filmed the previous year.

cards.heading: A marriage interrupted
cards.text: Rainer Werner Fassbinder's The Marriage of Maria Braun follows a woman building a place for herself in post-war West Germany while remaining attached to an absent husband. Hanna Schygulla plays Maria, who marries Hermann near the end of the war. The film premiered publicly at the Berlin International Film Festival on 20 February 1979, after being filmed the previous year.

cards.heading: Prosperity and postponement
cards.text: With Hermann missing, Maria finds ways to support herself through the disorder of the immediate post-war years. Her relationships become entangled with the work of survival and, later, with business success. She enters industrialist Karl Oswald's firm and becomes increasingly important to its operations. Material security grows around a marriage that is repeatedly postponed. The separation lets Maria preserve an idea of her life with Hermann even as her actual circumstances move further from it.

cards.heading: A private life inside reconstruction
cards.text: The screenplay by Peter Märthesheimer and Pea Fröhlich brings this private story into contact with the Federal Republic's economic recovery. Domestic interiors, commercial negotiations and voices from the radio make national events part of everyday experience. Schygulla's controlled performance gives Maria determination without making every motive explicit. Michael Ballhaus' photography helps organise the spaces in which people depend on one another, and Peer Raben's music adds to their uneasy emotional atmosphere. Schygulla received the Berlinale's acting award.

main.title: ZX80
main.summary: The Sinclair ZX80 is a home computer launched on 29 January 1980 by Science of Cambridge Ltd.

cards.heading: ZX80
cards.text:
The Sinclair ZX80 is a home computer launched on 29 January 1980 by Science of Cambridge Ltd. (later to be better known as Sinclair Research). It was one of the first computers available in the United Kingdom for less than a hundred pounds. It was available in kit form for £79.95, where purchasers had to assemble and solder it together, and as a ready-built version at £99.95.

The ZX80 was advertised as the first personal computer for under £100 and received praise for its value and documentation. However, it faced criticism for screen blanking during program execution, small RAM size, and the keyboard design. It was very popular straight away, and for some time there was a waiting list of several months for either version of the machine.

main.title: The Shining
main.summary: The Shining is a 1980 psychological horror film produced and directed by Stanley Kubrick and co-written with novelist Diane Johnson.

cards.heading: The Shining
cards.text:
The Shining is a 1980 psychological horror film produced and directed by Stanley Kubrick and co-written with novelist Diane Johnson. It is based on Stephen King's 1977 novel and stars Jack Nicholson, Shelley Duvall, Danny Lloyd and Scatman Crothers. The film presents the descent into insanity of a recovering alcoholic and aspiring novelist who takes a job as winter caretaker for a mountain resort hotel with his wife and clairvoyant son.

Production took place almost exclusively in England at EMI Elstree Studios, with sets based on real locations. Kubrick often worked with a small crew, which allowed him to do many takes, sometimes to the exhaustion of the actors and staff. The then-new Steadicam mount was used to shoot several scenes, giving the film an innovative and immersive look and feel.

main.title: BBC Micro
main.summary: The BBC Microcomputer System, or BBC Micro, is a family of microcomputers developed and manufactured by Acorn Computers in the early 1980s as part of the BBC's Computer Literacy Project.

cards.heading: BBC Micro
cards.text:
The BBC Microcomputer System, or BBC Micro, is a family of microcomputers developed and manufactured by Acorn Computers in the early 1980s as part of the BBC's Computer Literacy Project. Launched in December 1981, it was showcased across several educational BBC television programmes, such as The Computer Programme (1982), Making the Most of the Micro and Computers in Control (both 1983), and Micro Live (1985). Created in response to the BBC's call for bids for a microcomputer to complement its broadcasts and printed material, Acorn secured the contract with its rapidly prototyped "Proton" system, which was subsequently renamed the BBC Micro.

Although it was announced towards the end of 1981, production issues initially delayed the fulfilment of many orders, causing deliveries to spill over into 1982. Nicknamed the "Beeb", it soon became a fixture in British schools, advancing the BBC's goal of improving computer literacy.

main.title: NHK demonstrates HDTV in the United States
main.summary: NHK presented its experimental high-definition television system at the 1981 SMPTE conference in San Francisco.

cards.heading: More detail on television
cards.text:
NHK demonstrated its experimental high-definition television system at the SMPTE television conference in San Francisco in 1981. The presentation brought Japanese HDTV research before an American industry audience and helped widen international interest in higher-resolution television.

High-definition systems offered more image detail than conventional television. Their development raised questions about transmission capacity and shared production standards as broadcasters and manufacturers worked towards wider adoption.

main.title: IBM Personal Computer
main.summary: IBM released its Personal Computer, model 5150, on 12 August 1981.

cards.heading: IBM Personal Computer
cards.text: IBM released its Personal Computer, model 5150, on 12 August 1981. A team in Boca Raton developed the machine around Intel's 8088 processor, using an open architecture and components from outside suppliers. Expansion cards, peripherals and software gave other companies ways to build on the design. Its specifications became a widely adopted standard, creating the market for IBM PC-compatible computers. The consequences extended beyond one model: shared architectural features allowed hardware and software to reach machines from many manufacturers, shaping the personal computer market for decades.

main.title: Raiders of the Lost Ark
main.summary: Raiders of the Lost Ark is a 1981 American action-adventure film directed by Steven Spielberg and written by Lawrence Kasdan, based on a story by George Lucas and Philip Kaufman.

cards.heading: Raiders of the Lost Ark
cards.text:
Raiders of the Lost Ark is a 1981 American action-adventure film directed by Steven Spielberg and written by Lawrence Kasdan, based on a story by George Lucas and Philip Kaufman. Set in 1936, the film stars Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones, a globetrotting archaeologist vying with Nazi German forces to recover the long-lost Ark of the Covenant which is said to make an army invincible. Teaming up with his tough former romantic interest Marion Ravenwood (Karen Allen), Jones races to stop a rival archaeologist, René Belloq (Paul Freeman), from guiding the Nazis to the Ark and its power.

Lucas conceived Raiders of the Lost Ark in the early 1970s. Seeking to modernize the serial films of the early 20th century, he developed the idea further with Kaufman, who suggested the Ark as the film's goal. Lucas eventually focused on developing his 1977 film Star Wars. Development on Raiders of the Lost Ark resumed that year when he shared the idea with Spielberg, who joined the project several months later.

main.title: Blade Runner
main.summary: Ridley Scott's Blade Runner arrived in 1982, adapting Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?

cards.heading: Blade Runner
cards.text: Ridley Scott's Blade Runner arrived in 1982, adapting Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? In its future Los Angeles, former police officer Rick Deckard hunts escaped replicants, synthetic humans created to work in space colonies. The pursuit places him opposite Roy Batty and raises questions through their encounters. Vangelis's score accompanies the film's distinctive cityscape. Its initial North American release disappointed commercially and divided critics, with some questioning its pace. Later audiences helped establish it as a cult film and an influential work of science fiction cinema.

main.title: Commodore 64
main.summary: Commodore introduced the C64 in January 1982 and marketed it that August for 595 dollars.

cards.heading: Commodore 64
cards.text: Commodore introduced the C64 in January 1982 and marketed it that August for 595 dollars. Its name referred to 64 kibibytes of RAM, but custom graphics and sound hardware gave it much of its character. Multicolour sprites and a dedicated waveform-generation chip supported games and other software with distinctive images and audio. High production volumes helped it reach a broad home audience through the 1980s. Independent sales estimates range from 12.5 to 17 million machines, making the C64 one of personal computing's most widely owned models.
